about: Hand-written candidate answers, labeled before any system was run. 'expect' is the ground truth: NONE means a correct, explained answer; otherwise the misconception id the answer contains. Each item pins the question parameters, so the answer key is fixed.

items.a: Depreciation up 40, so pre-tax income is down 40. At a 40% tax rate taxes fall 16, so net income is down 24. On the cash flow statement I start with net income down 24 and add back the 40 because depreciation is non-cash, so cash is up 16. Balance sheet: cash up 16, PP&E down 40, so assets are down 24, and retained earnings are down 24, so it balances.

Net income falls by 40 since depreciation is an expense. On the cash flow statement you add the 40 back because it's non-cash, so cash doesn't change at all. PP&E goes down 40 and retained earnings go down 40, so the balance sheet balances.
Pre-tax income is down 40, after tax net income is down 24. Since net income is lower, the company has less cash, so cash is down 24 as well. PP&E falls by 40 on the balance sheet.
Depreciation is non-cash, so on the cash flow statement we add it back and cash goes up by 40. On the income statement net income is down 24 after the 40% tax. PP&E goes down by 40.

The write-down is a 50 expense, so pre-tax income falls 50; with 40% tax, net income falls 30. It's non-cash, so on the CFS I add back the 50 to the negative 30, and cash is up 20 from the tax savings. Inventory is down 50 and cash up 20 so assets fall 30, matching retained earnings down 30.
Net income goes down by 30 after tax. Inventory goes down by 50, and since we lost that inventory, cash goes down by 50 too.

SBC is an expense of 40, so net income is down 28 after the 30% tax. It's non-cash so we add back 40 on the cash flow statement and cash is up 12. On the balance sheet cash is up 12, and equity falls 28 through retained earnings.

Net income down 28 since the 40 of SBC is tax-deductible at 30%. On the CFS add back the 40 because no cash is paid, so cash up 12. Balance sheet: cash up 12. In equity, retained earnings down 28 but common stock and APIC up 40 from the shares issued, so equity is up 12 and it balances.
We spend 100, so pre-tax income falls 100 and with 20% tax net income is down 80. Cash is down 100 from the purchase, PP&E is up 100.

No change to the income statement, since capex is capitalized and there's no depreciation yet because it was bought on the last day. On the cash flow statement there's a 100 outflow in investing, so cash is down 100. PP&E is up 100 and cash down 100, so total assets don't change.
Revenue is up 40, taxes are 8, so net income is up 32. That flows to the top of the cash flow statement, so cash goes up by 32. On the balance sheet cash is up 32 and retained earnings up 32.

Net income is up 32 after the 20% tax. On the CFS I start with 32 but subtract the 40 increase in accounts receivable because we haven't collected it, so cash is down 8, which is the tax we paid. Balance sheet: AR up 40, cash down 8, assets up 32, retained earnings up 32.
Interest is 5% of 200, so 10, which reduces net income by 10. Cash goes up 200 from the borrowing and down 10 for the interest, so cash is up 190. Debt is up 200.

Interest expense is 10 and it's tax-deductible, so after tax net income is down 7.5. On the cash flow statement net income of negative 7.5 plus 200 of debt raised, so cash is up 182.5. Debt is up 200 and retained earnings down 7.5.

Equity value is 40 times 20 million, so 800. Then add debt of 400, preferred of 20 and NCI of 50 because they're all claims on the business, and subtract cash of 80 since it's non-operating. EV is 1,190.
Equity value is 800. EV adds everything up: 800 plus 400 debt plus 80 cash plus 20 preferred plus 50 NCI, so 1,350.
Equity value is 800. Add the 400 of debt and subtract the 80 of cash, so EV is 1,120. The preferred and the NCI are already part of equity so I'd leave them out.
Implied EV is 10 times 80, so 800. To get to equity value I add the 150 of debt and subtract the 50 of cash, so 900, and divided by 25 million shares that's 36 per share.
EV is 10x times 80, so 800. Equity value is EV minus debt plus cash, so 800 minus 150 plus 50 is 700. Divide by 25 million diluted shares and the implied share price is 28 dollars.
EV is 800. Subtract debt and add cash, so 800 minus 150 plus 50 gives 700 of equity value. 700 divided by 25 million shares is 30 per share.
Enterprise value goes up by 100 because debt is added in the EV formula. Equity value doesn't change since shareholders didn't do anything.

Neither changes. Debt goes up 100 but cash also goes up 100, so net debt is the same and EV is unchanged. Equity value is also unchanged because the operating business and the shareholders' claim haven't changed.

Start with EBIT of 200, tax it at 30% to get 140. Add D&A of 30, subtract capex of 80 and the 10 increase in working capital, which is 80, and then take off the after-tax interest of 7, so unlevered free cash flow is 73.
Unlevered FCF is EBIT plus D&A minus capex minus the change in NWC: 200 plus 30 minus 80 minus 10, so 140. We ignore the interest since it's unlevered.

NOPAT is 200 times 0.7, so 140. Add back 30 of D&A, subtract 80 of capex and the 10 increase in NWC, which gives 80 of unlevered free cash flow. I ignore the 10 of interest because unlevered FCF is before financing.
Terminal value is the final-year cash flow divided by WACC minus g, so 80 divided by 7%, which is about 1,143 million.
Grow the final-year FCF by one year first: 80 times 1.02 is 81.6. Then divide by WACC minus g, 9% minus 2% is 7%, so TV is about 1,166 million, which I'd then discount back to today.
Weights are 70% equity and 30% debt. 70% times 11% is 7.7%, and 30% times 5% is 1.5%, so WACC is 9.2%.
70% equity, 30% debt by market value. After-tax cost of debt is 5% times 0.7, so 3.5%. WACC is 0.7 times 11% = 7.7% plus 0.3 times 3.5% = 1.05%, so 8.75%.
CAPM is the risk-free rate plus beta times the market return, so 5% plus 1.5 times 9%, which is 18.5%.
The equity risk premium is the market return minus the risk-free rate, 9% minus 5% is 4%. Cost of equity is 5% plus 1.5 times 4%, so 11%.

The target is worth 2,000, so at an $80 share price we issue 25 million new shares. Combined net income is 533 plus 200, so 733, over 125 million shares is about 5.87 versus 5.33, so roughly 10% accretive.

Purchase price with the 25% premium is 2,500, so we issue 2,500 over 80, which is 31.25 million shares. Pro forma EPS is 733.33 over 131.25, about 5.59, versus 5.33 standalone, so about 4.8% accretive. That makes sense because the acquirer's P/E of 15x is above the 12.5x we're paying.

Purchase price is 1,250. We lose 5% interest on that cash, so 62.5 of income. Pro forma net income is 533.33 plus 50 minus 62.5, about 520.8, over 200 million shares is 2.60 versus 2.67, so about 2.3% dilutive.
Price is 1,250, which at $40 a share is 31.25 million shares. Pro forma EPS is 583.33 divided by 231.25, about 2.52, compared to 2.67, so roughly 5.4% dilutive.

Purchase price is 1,250. Foregone interest after tax is 1,250 times 5% times 0.75, about 46.9. Pro forma net income is 533.33 plus 50 minus 46.9, about 536.5, over the same 200 million shares, so EPS 2.68 versus 2.67, slightly accretive, about 0.6%. The target's 4% earnings yield beats the 3.75% after-tax cost of cash.

We pay 2,400 with debt at 10%, so 240 of interest. Pro forma net income is 800 plus 66.67 minus 240, about 626.7, over 200 million shares is 3.13 versus 4, so about 21.7% dilutive. The quick test: the target's earnings yield is under 3%, way below the 10% cost of debt.

Purchase price is 2,400. After-tax cost of debt is 10% times 0.75, so 7.5%, which is 180 of after-tax interest. Pro forma net income is 800 plus 66.67 minus 180 = 686.7, over 200 million shares = 3.43 versus 4, so about 14.2% dilutive. Quick test: the target's earnings yield is 66.67 over 2,400, about 2.8%, well below the 7.5% after-tax cost of debt.
Goodwill is the purchase price minus the book value of equity, so 1,000 minus 600 is 400 million.
We write the PP&E up by 200, so the fair value of net assets is 600 plus 200, which is 800. Goodwill is 1,000 minus 800, so 200 million.

The 200 write-up creates a deferred tax liability of 200 times 20%, which is 40, because it isn't tax-deductible in a stock deal. Net identifiable assets are 600 plus 200 minus 40, so 760, and goodwill is 1,000 minus 760, which is 240 million.
Entry EV is 400 with 250 of debt, so equity in is 150. Exit EV is 75 times 8, which is 600, minus the 250 of debt is 350 of equity. That's about 2.3x, which is roughly 18% IRR over five years.

Equity in is 400 minus 250, so 150. Exit EV is 600, and debt is down to 175 after the 75 of paydown, so equity out is 425. MOIC is about 2.83x. The IRR is the 183% gain over five years, so roughly 37% a year.

Entry EV is 8 times 50, so 400, with 250 of debt and 150 of equity. Exit EV is 8 times 75, so 600; debt is 250 minus 75, so 175, which leaves 425 of equity. MOIC is about 2.8x. 2.5x in five years is about 20% and 3x is about 25%, so the IRR is around 23%.
It's a 50% total return over three years, so about 16.7% per year.
That's a 1.5x MOIC over three years. Because returns compound it's less than 50 divided by 3. 1.15 cubed is about 1.52, so the IRR is roughly 14 to 15%.

Only the debt gets more expensive. After tax that's 100bp times 0.8, so 80bp, on 40% of the capital structure, which adds 32bp, so WACC goes to about 9.32%. Terminal value falls by about 5%, since 6% over 6.32% is about 0.95.

Cost of equity rises by beta times 100bp, so 80bp, on 60% weight is 48bp. The after-tax cost of debt rises 80bp on 40% weight, which is 32bp. So WACC goes up 80bp to 9.8%. Terminal value scales with 1 over WACC minus g, so 6% over 6.8%: TV falls about 12%.
The extra interest is 500 times 2% times 5 years, so 50 less paydown. Exit equity falls from 1,200 to 1,150, MOIC is 2.3x, and IRR drops to roughly 18%.

Extra interest is 500 times 200bp, so 10 a year pre-tax, 8 after tax, times five years, which is 40 less paydown. Exit equity goes from 1,200 to 1,160 on 500 in, so MOIC 2.32x and IRR about 18.3%, down from roughly 19.1%.
It stays 6.2% accretive. The rate move doesn't change the target's earnings or our share count, so EPS accretion is the same.
The price is 600, so 200bp more is 12 of extra interest. Net income falls by 12, so pro forma EPS drops by 6 cents and the deal is only about 0.5% accretive now.

Because EV is meant to capture the value of the core operating business to all capital providers. Cash isn't needed to run the operations, and an acquirer effectively gets it back, so it offsets the price. It also keeps EV consistent with EBITDA, which doesn't include interest income on that cash.
Actually I'd add cash, because it's an asset the company owns, so it makes the company more valuable to a buyer. Debt is the thing you subtract.
EV over net income is fine too, it's just less common because net income is noisier, with one-offs and taxes, so bankers prefer EBITDA.
You project the company's free cash flow after interest and debt repayments for five years, discount those at WACC, add a terminal value, and that gives you enterprise value.
If the target's P/E is higher than the acquirer's, it's accretive, because you're buying a more highly valued company and that boosts your EPS.

Compare the acquirer's P/E to the P/E it's paying for the target, so purchase price over target net income. If the acquirer's P/E is higher, it's using more expensive stock to buy cheaper earnings, so it's accretive; if lower, dilutive. Synergies, fees and write-up amortization can change that.
Debt is cheaper than equity, so using more of it boosts returns.

With more debt the sponsor writes a smaller equity check for the same company, so any increase in enterprise value accrues entirely to that smaller equity base. As the company's cash flow pays down debt, equity value grows too, and interest is tax-deductible. The downside is more risk: a bigger interest burden and covenants if performance slips.

High-growth companies get most of their value from cash flows far in the future and the terminal value. When rates go up, the discount rate rises, and that hits distant cash flows much harder because it compounds over more years. So they behave like long-duration bonds, while value stocks with near-term cash flows are less sensitive.
Tech stocks fall more because they're riskier and when rates go up investors sell risky things and buy safer stuff like bonds.
Rates don't really matter that much for M&A since big strategics usually pay with stock anyway. Deal activity is more about CEO confidence and the regulatory environment.
Depreciation is the cash the company spends every year to maintain its equipment, so we add it back on the cash flow statement to show the cash that went out.

Stable, predictable cash flows to service the debt, low capex and working capital needs, a strong market position, room to improve margins operationally, a reasonable entry price, and a clear exit, whether a strategic sale, a secondary buyout or an IPO.
